title: A retry helper that sleeps out the Retry-After delay gives a pure module a thread call
summary: The kernels in this module decide and never wait: the retry policy returns whether to retry, and the client's scheduler does the waiting. A developer adds a convenience that waits out the server's `Retry-After` delay with `Thread.sleep` and then decides, so that a client filter can retry inline. The module's capability contract, which lists every JDK capability its bytecode can reach, gains `threads`, and the build fails: the module can now block the thread it is called on.

change.description: Add `retryAfterWaiting`, which sleeps for the delay the server asked for and then returns `shouldRetry`. The existing method is untouched, the new one is a few lines, and it saves every caller from wiring a scheduler. No test is added, because the method is a sleep followed by a call that is already tested.

risk: A call that sleeps is a call that holds whatever thread it is on. In a servlet container that is one of a few hundred request threads, held for the length of a dependency's `Retry-After`, which under load is exactly when the dependency asks for long waits; the pool drains and the service stops answering requests that have nothing to do with that dependency. On a WebFlux event loop it is worse: one sleeping call stalls every request on that loop, and Reactor's `BlockHound` would have failed the call outright. Under virtual threads a `Thread.sleep` is cheap, which is why the change looks harmless on a laptop in 2026, and why it reaches production. The policy module was pure precisely so that it could be used from any of these without knowing which.
explanation: The capability contract of the module is derived from its compiled classes: every call from the module's bytecode to a JDK entry point of a capability (the clock, randomness, threads, the network, reflection, ...), grouped by capability. The committed contract says `threads: none`, which is the module's promise never to block, spawn or sleep. The patched bytecode calls `Thread.sleep` and `Thread.interrupt` from `RetryPolicy.retryAfterWaiting`, and the contract check lists both call sites. This is a closed-world check over every instruction, not a lint: bytecode that never names an entry point of a capability cannot exercise it. Deriving it takes milliseconds and needs no JVM.
resolution: Return the delay instead of waiting it out: `retryDelayMillis(...)` is as pure as `shouldRetry`, and the caller hands it to its own scheduler, `Mono.delay` on WebFlux, a `ScheduledExecutorService` or a virtual thread elsewhere. If a module really must gain a capability, `jvmcontract update` regenerates the contract and the diff names the new power and the call site, for a reviewer to approve.
provenance: Constructed from the blocking-call-in-a-library mistake that Reactor's BlockHound exists to catch, placed in the one module of a service that is meant to be callable from anywhere.

references.title: Reactor, BlockHound: detecting blocking calls from non-blocking threads
